title: Differentiated Instruction in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review of Research Evidence
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the evidence base for within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education. The authors note that differentiated instruction is widely promoted as a way to address student heterogeneity, but that its empirical support in secondary schools is unclear. The review asks what kinds of differentiated instruction have been studied in secondary education, how those approaches are operationalized, what effects they have on student academic achievement, and which contextual or personal factors appear to support or hinder effectiveness.

The paper uses a systematic review with a best-evidence synthesis approach covering literature from 2006 to 2016. The authors define differentiated instruction as planned adaptations to content, process, product, learning environment, or learning time based on assessed student needs. Included studies had to involve mainstream secondary education, use quantitative outcome measures of academic achievement, and compare differentiated instruction to business-as-usual or another condition. Fourteen papers representing 12 unique empirical studies met inclusion criteria. The reviewed interventions varied substantially, including generic teacher training in adaptive teaching, ability grouping and tiering, individualized instruction, mastery learning, heterogeneous grouping, and remediation in flipped classroom settings.

The population and context were mainstream secondary school students and teachers, with studies conducted across multiple regions including the United States, several European countries, Taiwan, and African countries. Subjects included mathematics, science, reading, and other academic domains. The review also considers school- and teacher-level conditions such as teacher knowledge, preparation time, collaboration, class size, and leadership support as possible moderators of implementation and outcomes.

The main conclusion is that differentiated instruction in secondary education shows small to moderate positive effects on student academic achievement overall, with summarized effect sizes ranging from d = +0.741 to +0.509 when omitting an outlier. However, the literature base is small, heterogeneous, and methodologically uneven, and differentiated instruction is operationalized in many different ways across studies. The authors therefore conclude that differentiated instruction appears promising, but stronger and more consistent research is still needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about which forms are most effective in secondary school settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using explicit inclusion criteria and quantitative effect-size synthesis, but it is not a clean meta-analysis of a single intervention and includes heterogeneous quasi-experimental and survey evidence with notable limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports mostly small to moderate positive effects on academic achievement, with synthesized effects generally above 0.20, indicating meaningful average impact for differentiated instruction overall.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 12 unique empirical studies (reported in 14 papers) on within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education, not AI tools. Across studies, the majority of findings were small to moderate positive effects on academic achievement, with summarized effect sizes reported as ranging roughly from d = +0.741 to +0.509 after omitting an outlier. Outcomes spanned multiple non-literacy academic domains including mathematics, science, and other school subjects, typically compared against business-as-usual or standard instruction.
finding.measure: Academic achievement tests across subject areas (e.g., mathematics, science, reading, other curriculum-aligned achievement measures)
finding.effect_size: range reported approximately d=+0.741 to +0.509 (with outlier omitted)
